# Correlation {#sec-correlation}

In correlation — or association analysis more generally — we can evaluate the
relationships between numeric variables. These variables can be taxonomic
features or patient metadata. For instance, we might be interested in which
taxonomic features are present simultaneously with others, or whether body
weight is associated with the abundance of certain features. In this chapter,
we will demonstrate how to perform correlation analysis with
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")`'s `getCrossAssociation()` method.

## Features vs. features

Here we demonstrate how to analyze which bacteria co-exists in the dataset.

```{r}
#| label: association1

library(mia)

data("peerj13075")
tse <- peerj13075

# Agglomerate to certain taxonomy level
tse <- agglomerateByPrevalence(tse, rank = "class")

# Apply clr-transform
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "clr", pseudocount = TRUE)

# Get correlation results
res <- getCrossAssociation(
    tse, tse,
    assay.type1 = "clr", assay.type2 = "clr",
    test.signif = TRUE, mode = "matrix"
)
```

We can visualize the result with a heatmap as we do later in this chapter, or
we can visualize the results with a correlation network plot as done below
(@fig-correlation-network).

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation-network
#| fig-cap: "Correlation network of the classes in the peerj13075 data, based on correlations between CLR-transformed abundances. Nodes are classes, and edge colour and width show the sign and strength of the correlation."
#| fig-alt: "Spring-layout network graph with one labelled node per class, connected by edges whose colour shows positive or negative correlation and whose width shows its strength."

library(qgraph)

# Create correlation network plot
qgraph(
    res$cor,
    layout = "spring", labels = colnames(res$cor),
    label.cex = 1.2, theme = "colorblind",
    node.width = 1.5, node.height = 2
)
```

You can find more on networks in the
[extra materials](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA-extras/docs/devel/pages/network_learning.html).

## Features vs. metadata

Now, we can calculate alpha diversity indices, and evaluate if they have
significant association with taxonomic features.

```{r}
#| label: association3

# Calculate diversity measures
index <- c(
    "shannon", "log_modulo_skewness", "coverage", "inverse_simpson", "gini"
)
tse <- addAlpha(tse, index = index)

# Get correlation results
res <- getCrossAssociation(
    tse, tse,
    assay.type1 = "clr", col.var2 = index,
    test.signif = TRUE, mode = "matrix"
)
```

Below, we present the results using a heatmap visualization with the help
of the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("ComplexHeatmap")` and
`r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("shadowtext")` R packages (@fig-correlation-taxa-alpha).

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation-taxa-alpha
#| fig-cap: "Heatmap of correlations between CLR-transformed abundances of classes (rows) and alpha diversity indices (columns) in the peerj13075 data. Significant correlations (adjusted p-value < 0.05) are marked with X."
#| fig-alt: "Clustered heatmap with classes as rows and five alpha diversity indices as columns, filled by correlation on a colour scale, with an X in the cells of significant correlations."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(shadowtext)

# Function for marking significant correlations with "X"
add_signif <- function(j, i, x, y, width, height, fill) {
    # If the p-value is under threshold
    if (!is.na(res$p_adj[i, j]) & res$p_adj[i, j] < 0.05) {
        # Print "X"
        grid.shadowtext(
            sprintf("%s", "X"), x, y,
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 8, col = "#f5f5f5")
        )
    }
}

# Create a heatmap
p <- Heatmap(res$cor,
    # Print values to cells
    cell_fun = add_signif,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(
        title = "correlation", legend_height = unit(5, "cm")
    ),
    column_names_rot = 45
)
p
```

## Metadata vs. metadata {#sec-alpha-correlation}

Finally, we demonstrate how to calculate correlation between sample metadata
variables. Here we estimate correlation between alpha diversity measures.

Compared to the solution in [@sec-compare-alpha], `getCrossAssociation()`
allows us to calculate correlations in bulk easily, without the need for
looping. The correlations are shown in @fig-correlation-alpha.

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation-alpha
#| fig-cap: "Heatmap of correlations between alpha diversity indices in the peerj13075 data. Significant correlations (adjusted p-value < 0.05) are marked with X."
#| fig-alt: "Clustered square heatmap with the five alpha diversity indices on both axes, filled by correlation on a colour scale, with an X in the cells of significant correlations."

# Get correlation results
res <- getCrossAssociation(
    tse, tse,
    col.var1 = index, col.var2 = index,
    test.signif = TRUE, mode = "matrix"
)

# Create a heatmap and store it
p <- Heatmap(res$cor,
    # Print values to cells
    cell_fun = add_signif,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(
        title = "correlation", legend_height = unit(5, "cm")
    ),
    column_names_rot = 45
)
p
```

## Exercises

**Goal:** After completing these exercises, you should be able to calculate
associations between taxonomic features and diversity.

**Exercise 1: Correlation**

1. Load any of the example data sets described in [@sec-data-sets].

2. Agglomerate the data to phylum level.

3. Apply the CLR transformation.

4. Calculate correlations of taxa abundances.

5. Visualize the correlation network. Are there taxonomic features whose
abundances are correlated?

6. Calculate all available alpha diversity indices with the un-agglomerated
data.

7. Calculate correlation between phyla and alpha diversity indices.

8. Visualize the correlation results with a heatmap. Are there taxonomic
features whose abundances associate with diversity? How would you interpret
this?

Useful functions:

`utils::data()`, `mia::agglomerateByRank`, `mia::transformAssay()`, `mia::getCrossAssociation()`,
`qgraph::qgraph()`, `mia::addAlpha()`, `ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap()`

:::
